newsitem.title: USA: Fifty years later, U.S. builds on Marshall Plan.
newsitem.headline: Fifty years later, U.S. builds on Marshall Plan.

text.p: Fifty years after the Marshall Plan, the United States is pressing another ambitious scheme, centred on NATO expansion, to ensure peace in Europe.

In reaching out to former communist countries excluded from the bold initiative that helped salvage Western Europe after the Second World War, Washington aims to finish the job of building an undivided, free, democratic and capitalist continent.

By enlarging NATO to include former members of the Warsaw Pact, "we want to do for Central and Eastern Europe what (former Secretary of State Dean) Acheson and (former Secretary of State George) Marshall did for the West, make war impossible," Strobe Talbott, deputy secretary of state, said.

The goals of the post-Second World War and post-Cold War initiatives -- peace and security -- are broadly similar, but the details associated with them are not. Controversy attended Marshall's vision then, and it surrounds NATO expansion now.
Marshall unveiled his plan for European recovery on June 5, 1947, in a Harvard University commencement address.

That paved the way for the United States to donate the equivalent of over $88 billion in today's dollars to 16 European countries between 1948 and 1952, according to Sir Leon Brittan of the European Commission.

President Bill Clinton and European leaders are expected to hail the programme during a summit next week in The Hague. And on June 5 Secretary of State Madeleine Albright addresses Harvard's newest graduates on the Marshall Plan's legacy.
Funnelling huge sums of U.S. aid into Germany, France, Britain, Italy and smaller countries after the Second World War was key to Europe's rehabilitation.

U.S. and other officials toyed with a similar plan for Russia after the Soviet Union's fall but rejected it because of budgetary pressures and concerns Russia did not have a capitalist system that would use the funds efficiently.

NATO expansion into Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and maybe other countries will cost billions of dollars for troops, new weapons and infrastructure. But aid is not the aim, and Washington, keen to share security costs, wants enlargement paid for by all its allies, new and old.

The United States was once the major source of European assistance. But from 1990 to 1996, the European Union and its member states gave former communist countries in Europe $58 billion in economic aid, compared with $12 billion from the United States, Brittan said in a Washington speech on May 5.
He and other experts say the Marshall Plan fostered European integration, which has quickened in recent years.
U.S. officials say NATO expansion aims to encourage EU enlargement and other processes linking European countries together and to the United States in a military, political and financial web.

Washington sees NATO expansion as a way to keep the alliance relevant after the Cold War's end, retain its trans-Atlantic leadership and continue transforming former communist states into democracies and trading partners.

The Marshall Plan proved the value of rebuilding wartime enemies like Germany, rather than exacting reparations and revenge. That lesson was used in the special agreement NATO and Washington will sign with Russia in Paris on May 27.
The Clinton administration welcomes European leadership much more than its predecessors did, but officials insist the United States remains the "indispensable nation, the sole superpower."

Some experts see evidence the Europeans are seeking to reduce that power, but others say Europe is so preoccupied with monetary union, scheduled for 1999, that its leaders may have little time in the near future to focus on issues outside the EU.
